items.title: The one-dimensional force models: data, motions, phase system, potential presentation, energy and equilibria
items.statement:
**(a) Data of a one-dimensional model.** A **one-dimensional model** is
declared by the following data: a fixed positive **mass** $m>0$, of dimension
$\mu$ read in kilograms ([[def-cm01-units]], [[post-cm01-worldlines]] clause
(v)); a **time window** $I_{0}\subseteq\mathbb R$, a nondegenerate open
interval read in seconds ([[def-interval]]); an open **configuration
domain** $Q\subseteq\mathbb R$, a nonempty open interval of the real line
read in metres; and a **force law**
$$F:I_{0}\times Q\times\mathbb R\longrightarrow\mathbb R,\qquad (t,x,v)\longmapsto F(t,x,v),$$
of dimension $\mu\ell\tau^{-2}$, read in newtons, subject to the **standing
regularity** of the framework: $F$ is continuous on $I_{0}\times Q\times
\mathbb R$ and locally Lipschitz in the state variable $(x,v)$ locally
uniformly in time ([[def-locally-lipschitz-in-the-state-variable]]). The
framework's three-dimensional force branch is
[[post-cm02-force-superposition]]; the class declared here is a **restricted
model class** adopted at the same primitive level, in which the physical
position of a single label along one coordinate is the whole state. A model
whose force law fails the standing regularity is not a one-dimensional model
of this class. When a statement differentiates the force law or the potential,
the additional smoothness it needs is stated in that statement.

**(b) Motions.** Let $J\subseteq I_{0}$ be an interval with nonempty interior
(endpoints read with one-sided derivatives, as in
[[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]). A **motion** of
the model on $J$ is a curve $x:J\to Q$ of class $C^{2}$
([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]) with
$$m\,x''(t)=F\bigl(t,x(t),x'(t)\bigr)\qquad(t\in J).$$
In the notation of the three-dimensional branch this is the scalar
restriction of its equation of motion clause (iv) to a single coordinate; the
motions of the present class are declared to be these curves. A **datum** at
time $t_{0}\in I_{0}$ is a triple $(t_{0},x_{0},v_{0})$ with $x_{0}\in Q$ and
$v_{0}\in\mathbb R$; a motion $x$ **takes** the datum when $x(t_{0})=x_{0}$
and $x'(t_{0})=v_{0}$.

**(c) Phase system.** The **phase system** of the model is the first-order
system on the open set $I_{0}\times Q\times\mathbb R\subseteq\mathbb R^{3}$
with right-hand side
$$G_{F}(t,x,v):=\Bigl(v,\ \frac{F(t,x,v)}{m}\Bigr),$$
read as a system of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]];
its state variable is $z=(x,v)$. For an interval $J\subseteq I_0$ with
nonempty interior, a **phase solution** on $J$ means a differentiable curve
$z:J\to Q\times\mathbb R$ satisfying $z'(t)=G_F(t,z(t))$ for every $t\in J$,
with domain-relative derivatives at included endpoints. Equivalently, for
any $t_0\in J$ it is a solution in the cited IVP sense with datum
$(t_0,z(t_0))$. For a $C^2$ curve $x:J\to Q$, being a motion is equivalent
to $t\mapsto(x(t),x'(t))$ being a phase solution: the first component is
$x'=v$ and the second is $x''=F(t,x,x')/m$. Conversely a phase solution
$(x,v)$ has $x'=v$ and $v'=F(t,x,v)/m$; continuity of $F$ makes $v'$ continuous,
so $x$ is $C^2$ and is a motion. This is the argument of clause (c) of
[[def-cm02-newtonian-flow]] read in one
coordinate. Here $x$ is the **position** or **displacement** coordinate and
$v$ the **velocity** coordinate; both are read in the fixed inertial frame in
which the model is declared. The phase system inherits the standing
regularity: $G_{F}$ is continuous and locally Lipschitz in the state variable
locally uniformly in time, so the Picard–Lindelöf hypotheses of
[[thm-picard-lindelof-local-existence-and-uniqueness]] hold at every point of
its domain.

**(d) Potential presentation, residual forces and energy.** The model
**presents its force law through a potential** when it declares a function
$U:Q\to\mathbb R$ of class $C^{2}$ in the sense of clause (a) of
[[def-cm03-potential-and-mechanical-energy]] of dimension
$\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$, read in joules, and a **residual force**
$d:I_{0}\times Q\times\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ of the standing regularity of
(a), with
$$F(t,x,v)=-U'(x)+d(t,x,v)\qquad\bigl((t,x,v)\in I_{0}\times Q\times\mathbb R\bigr);$$
here $U'$ is the ordinary derivative. This is the one-coordinate case of the
potential presentation of [[def-cm03-potential-and-mechanical-energy]] clause
(a) for a time- and velocity-independent potential, and the scalar
$U$ is a **potential energy** of the model's potential part. The model is a
**global potential model** (equivalently, in the framework's usage, a
**conservative model**) when $d\equiv0$; the term "conservative" is used only
in this sense, as recorded in that definition. For a conservative model the
**mechanical energy** is the function
$$E:Q\times\mathbb R\longrightarrow\mathbb R,\qquad E(x,v):=\tfrac12 m v^{2}+U(x),$$
of dimension $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$. For a model with declared residual
forces, the **mechanical energy along a motion** $x:J\to Q$ is
$E(t):=\tfrac12m\,x'(t)^{2}+U(x(t))$; it is defined along curve families even
though the force law is not presented through $U$ alone.

**(e) Equilibria.** A **time- and velocity-independent force law** on $Q$ is
one of the form $F(t,x,v)=f(x)$ for a function $f:Q\to\mathbb R$; the model
is then **autonomous**. For such a law, a point $x_{*}\in Q$ is an
**equilibrium** (or **rest position**) when $f(x_{*})=0$, and the phase-plane
point $(x_{*},0)$ is the corresponding **rest point** of the phase system;
the constant curve $x\equiv x_{*}$ is then a motion. When the force law is
presented as $f=-U'$ with $U$ of class $C^{2}$, the equilibria are exactly
the critical points of $U$:
$f(x_{*})=0\iff U'(x_{*})=0$. A point $x_{0}\in Q$ is a **strict local
minimum** of $U$ when $U(x)>U(x_{0})$ for every $x\in Q$ with $0<\lvert
x-x_{0}\rvert<r_{0}$ for some $r_{0}>0$. The **Lyapunov stability** and
**asymptotic stability** of a rest point of the autonomous phase system are
the notions of [[def-cm-equilibrium-and-lyapunov-stability]] applied to the
field $G_{F}$; they are not defined here anew.

**(f) Oscillator-type data.** Let $m>0$, $c\ge0$, $k\in\mathbb R$ and let
$f:I_{0}\to\mathbb R$ be continuous. A model **is of oscillator type with
data $(m,c,k,f)$** when its force law has the form
$$F(t,x,v)=f(t)-c\,v-k\,x\qquad\bigl((t,x,v)\in I_{0}\times Q\times\mathbb R\bigr)$$
with $Q$ a nonempty open interval containing $0$ when the equation is read
about the origin, and the parameters are read with dimensions $[c]=\mu\tau^{-1}$
(kilograms per second), $[k]=\mu\tau^{-2}$ (kilograms per second squared) and
$[f]=\mu\ell\tau^{-2}$ (newtons). For such a model the equation of motion is
the second-order equation $m\,x''+c\,x'+k\,x=f(t)$, and the motions are
exactly the restrictions of the solutions of the mathematical model of
[[def-cm-oscillator-model-and-phase-system]] with the same data, by the
identification of that definition's phase system with the phase system (c).
The parameters $c$ and $k$ are model data: they enter the model's declaration
and are not derived by this item.

**(g) Status.** This item introduces vocabulary, objects, regularity and
dimensions; it contains no existence, uniqueness, conservation, stability or
boundedness assertion, no force law of nature and no measured value. In
particular, clause (a) **declares** the one-dimensional class rather than
deriving it from the three-dimensional branch, and clauses (d)-(f) only fix
which data a model of the class carries. Every later statement of this page
names the model data, the potential representative and the initial datum it
uses.
items.strategy: A definition: it declares the one-dimensional model class (mass, time window, configuration interval, force law with the standing regularity), its motions and phase system, the potential presentation with residual forces and the mechanical energy, the equilibria and the strict-minimum vocabulary, and the oscillator-type data (m,c,k,f), with domains, regularity and dimensions; it adopts no force law and asserts no dynamical statement.
items.physical_scope: The declared one-dimensional model class of the framework: a single scalar coordinate with an open configuration interval, a fixed positive mass, and a scalar force law with the standing continuity and state-Lipschitz regularity; the motions, the phase system, the potential presentation with a scalar potential and residual forces, the mechanical energy, the equilibria of a time- and velocity-independent force law, and the oscillator-type data (m,c,k,f). The item fixes vocabulary, domains, regularity and dimensions for the conservative and dissipative models of this page; it adopts no force law of nature, asserts no existence, uniqueness, conservation or stability statement, and records no measured value.

items.title: The phase plane of a one-dimensional model: phase curves, the energy function and its level sets, and turning points
items.statement:
Adopt a one-dimensional model $(m,I_{0},Q,F)$ of
[[def-cm04-one-dimensional-models-and-equilibria]], with phase system
$G_{F}(t,x,v)=(v,F(t,x,v)/m)$.

**(a) Phase plane and phase curves.** The **phase plane** of the model is
$\mathbb R^{2}$ with coordinates $(x,v)$, where $x$ is the position and $v$
the velocity coordinate of clause (b) of [[def-cm04-one-dimensional-models-and-equilibria]].
They are real numerical SI coordinates: if $X_{\rm phys}$ and $V_{\rm phys}$
are the corresponding physical position and velocity, then
$x=X_{\rm phys}/(1\,\mathrm m)$ and
$v=V_{\rm phys}/(1\,\mathrm{m/s})$ ([[def-cm01-units]]). The **phase domain**
of the model is the open set $I_{0}\times Q\times\mathbb R$ of (time,
position, velocity) triples. The phase plane is read with the Euclidean
structure and norm $\lVert(x,v)\rVert_{2}=\sqrt{x^{2}+v^{2}}$ on these
dimensionless numerical coordinates ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]);
physical displacement and velocity are not added as dimensionful quantities.
Distances used below are those of this norm. For a curve family
$x:J\to Q$ of class $C^{1}$ its **phase curve** is
$t\mapsto(x(t),x'(t))$; when $x$ is a motion of the model the phase curve is
the corresponding solution of the phase system.

**(b) The energy function of a conservative model.** Let the model be a
global potential model of clause (d) of
[[def-cm04-one-dimensional-models-and-equilibria]] with potential $U$ of
class $C^{2}$, so that $F=-U'$. The **energy function** of the model is
$$E:Q\times\mathbb R\longrightarrow\mathbb R,\qquad E(x,v):=\tfrac12 m v^{2}+U(x),$$
of dimension $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$ (joules). For $E_{0}\in\mathbb R$ the
**energy level set** of $E_{0}$ and the **energy sublevel set** of $E_{0}$
are
$$\Sigma_{E_{0}}:=\{(x,v)\in Q\times\mathbb R:E(x,v)=E_{0}\},\qquad S_{E_{0}}:=\{(x,v)\in Q\times\mathbb R:E(x,v)\le E_{0}\}.$$

**(c) Turning positions and turning points.** Let the model be as in (b).
A point $x\in Q$ is a **turning position** of the energy $E_{0}$ when
$U(x)=E_{0}$, and the phase-plane point $(x,0)$ is the corresponding
**turning point** of $E_{0}$. A turning position at which $U'$ does not
vanish is a **simple turning position**. In the one-coordinate reading of
[[def-cm-mechanical-vector-field-and-energy-in-a-chart]] the potential
difference $U(x)-E_{0}$ is the sign-controlling quantity for the velocity of
a motion of energy $E_{0}$; the statements of that kind are the content of
the conservation theorem of this page and are not made here.

**(d) Rest points and stability vocabulary.** For a model with a time- and
velocity-independent force law $f$, the equilibria, rest points, strict local
minima and the Lyapunov and asymptotic stability of a rest point are those of
clause (e) of [[def-cm04-one-dimensional-models-and-equilibria]], read for
the phase system $G_{F}$; Lyapunov stability is the notion of
[[def-cm-equilibrium-and-lyapunov-stability]] and linear stability is that of
[[def-cm-orbital-and-linear-stability]], applied to $G_{F}$ at its rest
point. For an oscillator-type model with data $(m,c,k,f)$ of clause (f) of
[[def-cm04-one-dimensional-models-and-equilibria]] the phase system is the
phase-plane system of [[def-cm-oscillator-model-and-phase-system]], and the
phase-plane reading of its equilibria is the one recorded there.

**(e) Status.** This item fixes geometric objects and reads mathematical
stability vocabulary for the scalar phase system; it asserts no conservation
of energy, no containment of a phase curve in a level set, no boundedness of
level sets and no measured value.
items.strategy: A definition: it fixes the phase plane with its position and velocity coordinates, the phase curve of a motion, the energy function of a conservative model with its level and sublevel sets, turning positions and points, and the reading of the equilibrium and stability vocabulary for the scalar phase system; it asserts no conservation or boundedness statement.
items.physical_scope: The geometric vocabulary of the one-dimensional models of this page: the phase plane with position and velocity expressed as numerical SI coordinates, the Euclidean norm on that normalized pair, the phase curve of a motion, the mechanical energy function of a conservative model, its energy level sets and sublevel sets, and turning positions and turning points. The item also fixes how the equilibrium, Lyapunov-stability and linear-stability vocabulary of the mathematical definitions is read for the scalar phase system. It asserts no conservation, no containment of phase curves in level sets, no boundedness and no measured value; those are statements of the theorems of this page.

items.title: The harmonic (linear restoring) model: a declared linear force law with parameter $k>0$
items.statement:
**(i) Setting.** Work in the one-dimensional model class of
[[def-cm04-one-dimensional-models-and-equilibria]] with time window
$I_{0}=\mathbb R$, configuration domain $Q=\mathbb R$, a fixed mass $m>0$
and a **spring constant** $k>0$ of dimension $\mu\tau^{-2}$, read in newtons
per metre ([[def-cm01-units]]). The **harmonic model** is the model whose
force law is the **linear restoring force**
$$F(x,v):=-k\,x .$$
Its equation of motion is $m\,x''=-k\,x$, equivalently $m\,x''+k\,x=0$; the
model is autonomous and velocity-independent, and its potential is
$$U(x):=\tfrac12 k\,x^{2},$$
of dimension $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$ (joules), which presents the force law in
the sense of clause (d) of [[def-cm04-one-dimensional-models-and-equilibria]]:
$U$ is of class $C^{2}$ in that clause's sense, and
$-U'(x)=-k\,x=F(x)$ ([[lem-derivative-of-a-power]],
[[def-derivative]]). The harmonic model is therefore a **conservative**
model of the class, with the potential representative $U$ declared above and
no residual force.

**(ii) Regularity and framework status.** Let
$X:=x_{\rm phys}/(1\,\mathrm m)$ and
$V:=v_{\rm phys}/(1\,\mathrm{m/s})$ be the dimensionless numerical SI state
coordinates (the real state coordinates in the displayed force-map signature),
and let $K:=k_{\rm phys}/(1\,\mathrm{N/m})$ be the numerical
spring constant. In this representation the numerical force map
$\widehat F:=F_{\rm phys}/(1\,\mathrm N)$ is
$\widehat F(X,V)=-KX$, so
$\lvert\widehat F(X,V)-\widehat F(X',V')\rvert\le
K\,\lVert(X,V)-(X',V')\rVert_{2}$. It is therefore locally Lipschitz in the
state variable with global numerical-coordinate constant $K$, uniformly in
time ([[def-locally-lipschitz-in-the-state-variable]]). The harmonic model is
thus an admissible model of the class of clause (a) of
[[def-cm04-one-dimensional-models-and-equilibria]], and the existence,
uniqueness and conservation statements of this page apply to it. It is
adopted as a restricted model class of the framework, at the same primitive
level as the force maps of [[post-cm02-force-superposition]]: the force law
is model input.

**(iii) Physical reading and regime.** The model idealizes a **restoring
force linear in the displacement**: an ideal spring, or the quadratic
approximation of a potential $U$ near a strict local minimum $x_{*}$ with $U''(x_*)>0$, where
the Taylor expansion of the effective potential begins with the quadratic
term $\tfrac12 U''(x_{*})(x-x_{*})^{2}$ and the linearized equation carries
the **effective spring constant** $U''(x_{*})$ (the sources' linearization
procedure). The model is adopted for a stated regime — displacements so
small that the neglected remainder of the potential is adequate for the
purpose at hand — and it is **not** claimed to describe large-amplitude
oscillations, nonlinear springs, plasticity, or any given real system. The
coefficient $k$ is a model parameter, not a constant of the framework; when
its value is taken from a calibration experiment, that value is an empirical
premise carrying the apparatus conditions and the measurement uncertainty,
and the framework asserts none of it here. The linear form is the simplest
restoring law satisfying the standing regularity; that is a modelling
convenience, not a derivation.

**(iv) Status.** Adopted assumption of the framework when a model invokes
it; it selects no law of nature on its own. Every consequence below is a
conditional statement about the declared equation of motion.
items.strategy: Adoption of the harmonic model: the linear restoring force -kx with declared spring constant k>0 and potential kx^2/2, with its regularity check, its reading as the quadratic approximation at a strict minimum of a potential, its regime of validity, and the status of k as model data.
items.physical_scope: Adoption of the harmonic oscillator as a restricted one-dimensional model: configuration domain the whole line, fixed mass m>0, force law F(x)=-k x with declared spring constant k>0 of dimension mass per time squared, and potential U(x)=k x^2/2. The model is a linear idealization of a restoring force, adopted for a stated regime (small displacements from a stable equilibrium, in which the quadratic term of the potential is the adequate approximation, as in the sources' linearization procedure); the spring constant is model data whose value, if taken from measurement, is an empirical premise with its own conditions and uncertainty. The item asserts no value of k, no claim that the model applies to a given spring or oscillation, and no measured result.

items.title: Existence, uniqueness and conservation of energy for a one-dimensional conservative model: phase curves lie in energy level sets and the velocity is determined by the position and energy up to sign
items.statement:
Adopt a **conservative one-dimensional model**: the class of clause (a) of
[[def-cm04-one-dimensional-models-and-equilibria]] with a **time- and
velocity-independent** force law presented through a potential, that is
$$F(x)=-U'(x)\qquad(x\in Q)$$
for a function $U:Q\to\mathbb R$ of class $C^{2}$ (so the residual force of
clause (d) of that definition vanishes identically and the model is a global
potential model). Write
$$E(x,v)=\tfrac12 m v^{2}+U(x)$$
for the energy function of [[def-cm04-phase-plane-and-energy-level-sets]]
clause (b). Then:

1. **Existence and uniqueness.** Every datum $(t_{0},x_{0},v_{0})$ with
   $t_{0}\in I_{0}$, $x_{0}\in Q$, $v_{0}\in\mathbb R$ has exactly one
   **maximal motion**: a motion $x:J_{\max}\to Q$ with $x(t_{0})=x_{0}$ and
   $x'(t_{0})=v_{0}$ that has no extension to a motion on a strictly larger
   interval. Its interval $J_{\max}$ is open, contains $t_{0}$ and is
   contained in $I_{0}$, and every motion of the model with the same datum is
   the restriction of $x$ to a subinterval.
2. **Energy conservation.** For every motion $x:J\to Q$ the function
   $t\mapsto E(x(t),x'(t))$ is constant on $J$.
3. **Level-set containment and velocity determination.** Let $x:J\to Q$ be
   a motion with datum $(t_{0},x_{0},v_{0})$ and let $E_{0}:=E(x_{0},v_{0})$.
   Then $U(x(t))\le E_{0}$ for every $t\in J$; if $U(x(t))<E_{0}$ then
   $$x'(t)=\pm\sqrt{\frac{2\bigl(E_{0}-U(x(t))\bigr)}{m}},$$
   the two signs giving the only two possible values; and $x'(t)=0$ holds
   exactly when $U(x(t))=E_{0}$. In particular the phase curve of $x$ is
   contained in the energy level set $\Sigma_{E_{0}}$ of clause (b) of
   [[def-cm04-phase-plane-and-energy-level-sets]].
4. **Rest motions.** A point $x_{*}\in Q$ is an equilibrium of the model if
   and only if $U'(x_{*})=0$; in that case the constant curve
   $x\equiv x_{*}$ is the maximal motion with datum $(t_{0},x_{*},0)$, and
   conversely the maximal motion with datum $(t_{0},x_{*},0)$ is constant
   exactly when $U'(x_{*})=0$.

The statement is conditional on the declared potential $U$: replacing $U$ by
$U+c$ with a constant $c$ changes $E$ on the whole phase plane by $c$ and
leaves clauses 1, 3 and 4 unchanged. No claim of periodicity, boundedness of
the position or of the velocity, or approach to an equilibrium is made.
items.strategy: A conditional deduction: apply the maximal-solution theorem to the phase system for existence and uniqueness, differentiate the energy along a motion using the equation of motion to obtain conservation, and read off the level-set containment, the velocity determination and the correspondence between rest points and equilibria.
items.physical_scope: The basic dynamical content of a conservative one-dimensional model: every datum has exactly one maximal motion; the mechanical energy m x-dot^2/2 + U(x) is constant along every motion; a motion of initial energy E_0 keeps its position in the sublevel set {U <= E_0}, and where U is strictly below E_0 its velocity is one of the two square-root values determined by the position and E_0; every non-turning phase point of the motion lies on the energy level set of E_0; and the constant motions are exactly the rest motions at equilibria. The result is a conditional deduction from the declared potential presentation; it asserts no periodicity, no boundedness of the motion, no asymptotic behaviour and no measured value.

items.title: A strict local minimum of the potential is a Lyapunov stable equilibrium of the conservative one-dimensional model, and its linearisation is an oscillator-type model
items.statement:
Adopt a conservative one-dimensional model as in
[[pthm-cm04-conservative-motion-and-energy]]: the class of
[[def-cm04-one-dimensional-models-and-equilibria]] with force law
$F(x)=-U'(x)$ for a potential $U:Q\to\mathbb R$ of class $C^{2}$, phase
system $G_{F}(x,v)=(v,-U'(x)/m)$ on $Q\times\mathbb R$, and energy
$E=\tfrac12mv^{2}+U$. Let $x_{*}\in Q$ be a **strict local minimum** of $U$:
there is $r_{0}>0$ with $\overline B(x_{*},r_{0})\subseteq Q$ and
$U(x)>U(x_{*})$ for $0<\lvert x-x_{*}\rvert<r_{0}$. Then:

1. **Lyapunov stability.** $(x_{*},0)$ is a Lyapunov stable rest point of
   the phase system in the sense of [[def-cm-equilibrium-and-lyapunov-stability]]:
   for every $\varepsilon>0$ with $\overline B((x_{*},0),\varepsilon)\subseteq
   Q\times\mathbb R$ there is $\delta>0$ such that the unique maximal solution of the autonomous phase equation through the datum of every motion $x$ of the
   model with $\lVert(x(t_{0}),x'(t_{0}))-(x_{*},0)\rVert_{2}<\delta$ for some
   $t_{0}\in I_{0}$ is defined for all $t\ge t_{0}$ and satisfies
   $$\bigl\lVert\bigl(x(t)-x_{*},\,x'(t)\bigr)\bigr\rVert_{2}<\varepsilon \qquad(t\ge t_{0}).$$
   Here $x$ in the displayed all-time bound denotes that maximal extension; on the original motion interval it agrees with the given motion. The autonomous equation is read on $\mathbb R\times Q\times\mathbb R$, even when the declared time window $I_0$ is smaller; no enlargement of that declared window is asserted. The norm is the Euclidean norm on $\mathbb R^{2}$ of
   [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]; the balls are those of
   [[def-metric-ball]]. No asymptotic stability and no attraction are
   asserted.

2. **Linearisation.** $U''(x_{*})$ exists ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]),
   the phase field $G_{F}$ is totally differentiable at $(x_{*},0)$ with
   $$DG_{F}(x_{*},0)(\delta x,\delta v)=\Bigl(\delta v,\ -\frac{U''(x_{*})}{m}\,\delta x\Bigr),$$
   and the linearised equation is
   $$m\,\xi''+U''(x_{*})\,\xi=0,$$
   which is the equation of the oscillator-type model of clause (f) of
   [[def-cm04-one-dimensional-models-and-equilibria]] with data
   $(m,0,U''(x_{*}),0)$ ([[def-cm-oscillator-model-and-phase-system]]). If in
   addition $U''(x_{*})>0$, then that linearised model is the harmonic model
   of [[post-cm04-harmonic-model]] with spring constant $U''(x_{*})$, and its
   undamped frequency in the sense of
   [[def-cm-oscillator-model-and-phase-system]] is $\sqrt{U''(x_{*})/m}$.

The statement is conditional on the potential $U$ and on the strict local
minimum; no conclusion is drawn for a critical point that is only a weak
minimum, a maximum, or a point where $U''$ vanishes identically on one side.

The statement is conditional on the declared potential and its strict local minimum; it asserts no asymptotic stability, no attraction and no instability in any case, and no measured value.

items.title: The motions of the harmonic model are the sinusoids $A\cos(\omega(t-t_0))+B\sin(\omega(t-t_0))$: amplitude and phase, the least period, the conserved energy $kR^2/2$ and the elliptical phase curves
items.statement:
Adopt the harmonic model of [[post-cm04-harmonic-model]]: the
one-dimensional model of [[def-cm04-one-dimensional-models-and-equilibria]]
with $m>0$, $k>0$, force law $F(x)=-kx$ and potential $U(x)=\tfrac12kx^{2}$.
Write
$$\omega:=\sqrt{\frac{k}{m}}>0$$
for its **undamped frequency** in the sense of
[[def-cm-oscillator-model-and-phase-system]]. Then:

1. **Motions.** Let $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with nonempty
   interior and let $t_{0}\in J$. A curve $x:J\to\mathbb R$ is a motion of the
   model on $J$ if and only if there are reals $A,B$ with
   $$x(t)=A\cos\bigl(\omega(t-t_{0})\bigr)+B\sin\bigl(\omega(t-t_{0})\bigr) \qquad(t\in J).$$
   For every datum $(t_{0},x_{0},v_{0})$ there is exactly one maximal motion,
   it is defined on all of $\mathbb R$, and its coefficients are
   $A=x_{0}$, $B=v_{0}/\omega$; every motion with that datum is its
   restriction.
All claims involving every real time, periods or the whole phase ellipse below refer to the unique maximal extension of clause 1; on a local motion interval the same formulas hold by restriction.

2. **Amplitude and phase.** With $A,B$ as in clause 1 put
   $R:=\sqrt{A^{2}+B^{2}}$. Then $\lvert x(t)\rvert\le R$ for every $t$; if
   $R>0$ there is a real $\varphi$ with $\cos\varphi=A/R$ and
   $\sin\varphi=B/R$, and then
   $$x(t)=R\cos\bigl(\omega(t-t_{0})-\varphi\bigr)\qquad(t\in\mathbb R).$$
   If $R=0$ the motion is the rest motion $x\equiv0$.
3. **Period and frequency.** For every motion $x(t+T)=x(t)$ holds for all
   $t$ whenever $\omega T\in2\pi\mathbb Z$. If $R>0$, conversely every
   period $T>0$ of $x$ satisfies $\omega T\in2\pi\mathbb Z$, so the **least
   positive period** of the motion is $T_{\mathrm{per}}=2\pi/\omega$, and the
   **frequency** in cycles per second is $f=1/T_{\mathrm{per}}=\omega/(2\pi)$.
   If $R=0$ every $T$ is a period.
4. **Energy and phase curves.** Along every motion with coefficients $A,B$
   the mechanical energy is
   $$E\bigl(x(t),x'(t)\bigr)=\tfrac12k\bigl(A^{2}+B^{2}\bigr)=\tfrac12kR^{2}$$
   for every $t$, the phase curve is contained in the ellipse
   $$\Sigma_{R}:=\Bigl\{(x,v)\in\mathbb R^{2}:\frac{x^{2}}{R^{2}}+\frac{v^{2}}{\omega^{2}R^{2}}=1\Bigr\}$$
   when $R>0$, and it is exactly that ellipse: every point of $\Sigma_{R}$
   lies on the phase curve of the motion and is attained at exactly the times
   $t=t_{0}+\bigl(\theta_{1}+\varphi+2\pi n\bigr)/\omega$, $n\in\mathbb Z$,
   for the appropriate $\theta_{1}$. For $R=0$ the phase curve is the single
   point $(0,0)$, which is also the level set of energy $0$.
5. **Rest point.** The origin $(0,0)$ is the only rest point of the model,
   and it is Lyapunov stable, by
   [[pthm-cm04-equilibrium-stability-at-a-strict-minimum]]; no asymptotic
   stability is asserted.

The statement uses the declared data $m,k$ only through $\omega$ and the
energy; no value of $m$ or $k$ is asserted, and no real oscillator is claimed
to obey the model.
items.strategy: A direct deduction: transport the mathematical classification of the homogeneous oscillator to an arbitrary base time, prove the unit-circle parametrisation used for the phase form and the ellipse coverage, compute the energy along the explicit family, read the least period from the fundamental period of cosine, and apply the strict-minimum theorem at the origin.
items.physical_scope: The complete motion analysis of the harmonic model with m>0 and k>0: every motion is a sinusoid about any chosen base time, with the initial data as coefficients; the amplitude and phase form; the least period 2 pi/omega and the frequency in cycles per second; the conserved mechanical energy k R^2/2; the phase curve is exactly the ellipse of the energy level set, with the two semiaxes; and the origin is the unique rest point and is Lyapunov stable. The result is a conditional deduction from the adopted linear force law; it asserts no value of k or m, no application to a real spring, and no asymptotic stability.

items.title: The damped oscillator model: a harmonic restoring force with a phenomenological linear drag $-c\dot x$, $c\ge0$
items.statement:
**(i) Setting.** Work in the one-dimensional model class of
[[def-cm04-one-dimensional-models-and-equilibria]] with time window
$I_{0}=\mathbb R$, configuration domain $Q=\mathbb R$, a fixed mass $m>0$,
the spring constant $k>0$ of [[post-cm04-harmonic-model]], and a **drag
coefficient** $c\ge0$ of dimension $\mu\tau^{-1}$, read in kilograms per
second ([[def-cm01-units]]). The model's force law is declared through the
additive composition of force contributions, in the sense of clause (v) of
[[post-cm02-force-superposition]], read in one coordinate:
$$F(x,v)=-k\,x-c\,v .$$

The **damped oscillator model** is the one-dimensional model with this force
law; its equation of motion is
$$m\,x''+c\,x'+k\,x=0,$$
and its data $(m,c,k,0)$ are oscillator-type data in the sense of clause (f)
of [[def-cm04-one-dimensional-models-and-equilibria]]. The model is
autonomous and depends on the velocity; it is **undamped** when $c=0$, in
which case it is exactly the harmonic model of [[post-cm04-harmonic-model]],
and **strictly damped** when $c>0$.

**(ii) Potential presentation with a residual force.** The model presents its
force law through the harmonic potential $U(x)=\tfrac12kx^{2}$ of
[[post-cm04-harmonic-model]] together with the **residual force**
$$d(t,x,v)=-c\,v,$$
in the sense of clause (d) of [[def-cm04-one-dimensional-models-and-equilibria]]:
$F(x,v)=-U'(x)+d(t,x,v)$. The mechanical energy of the model is therefore
the function $E(x,v)=\tfrac12mv^{2}+\tfrac12kx^{2}$ of clause (d), defined
along every motion; the drag force is not presented through a potential and
the model is not a global potential model when $c>0$.

**(iii) Regularity.** Let
$X:=x_{\rm phys}/(1\,\mathrm m)$ and
$V:=v_{\rm phys}/(1\,\mathrm{m/s})$ be the dimensionless numerical SI state
coordinates (the real state coordinates in the displayed force-map signature),
and let $K:=k_{\rm phys}/(1\,\mathrm{N/m})$,
$C:=c_{\rm phys}/(1\,\mathrm{kg/s})$ be the numerical coefficients. The
numerical force map $\widehat F:=F_{\rm phys}/(1\,\mathrm N)$ is
$\widehat F(X,V)=-KX-CV$, so
$$\lvert\widehat F(X,V)-\widehat F(X',V')\rvert\le K\lvert X-X'\rvert+C\lvert V-V'\rvert\le(K+C)\,\lVert(X,V)-(X',V')\rVert_{2}.$$
The real number $K+C$ is a Lipschitz constant for this normalized numerical
coordinate map; the dimensionful coefficients $k$ and $c$ are not added.
The force map is continuous and locally Lipschitz in the state variable,
uniformly in time ([[def-locally-lipschitz-in-the-state-variable]]). It is an
admissible force law of the class of clause (a) of
[[def-cm04-one-dimensional-models-and-equilibria]], and its equation is
exactly the homogeneous model $m\,x''+cx'+kx=0$ of
[[def-cm-oscillator-model-and-phase-system]].

**(iv) Physical status and regime.** The drag term is a **phenomenological**
constitutive model, adopted rather than derived: it represents the net force
of a medium whose microscopic state is not part of the model. The linear
velocity-proportional form is a restricted regime — slow motion through a
viscous medium, of which the Stokes force $c=6\pi\eta a$ is the recorded
example in the framework's drag postulate [[post-cm02-drag]] — and the
coefficient $c$ is a model parameter depending on body and medium. Other
regimes are different models: drag growing quadratically with speed, or
Coulomb sliding friction, whose force contains the factor $v/\lvert v\rvert$
and is undefined at $v=0$ and is not of the standing regularity. The model
also neglects the random component of the environment's force; the recorded
source states that this neglect is admissible only in a stated energy regime,
in which the oscillator's energy greatly exceeds the energy scale of the
environment's fluctuations. No value of $c$, $m$ or $k$ is asserted, and a
measured value used in an application is an empirical premise with its own
conditions and uncertainty.

**(v) Status.** Adopted assumption of the framework when a model invokes it;
the damped oscillator selects no law of nature on its own, and no
fluctuation–dissipation relation is asserted. Its conditional consequences
are the subject of the damped-motion theorems of this page.
items.strategy: Adoption of the damped oscillator model: the harmonic restoring force composed with the phenomenological linear drag -cv of declared coefficient c>=0, with its potential-plus-residual presentation, its regularity, its viscous regime of validity and the neglected environment fluctuations.
items.physical_scope: Adoption of the damped oscillator as a restricted one-dimensional model: the harmonic restoring force with spring constant k>0 combined, through additive composition of force contributions, with a linear drag force -c x-dot of declared drag coefficient c>=0 (kilograms per second). The drag term is phenomenological: it represents the net effect of a medium that is not modelled, is adopted for a stated regime (viscous, velocity-proportional resistance at small speeds), neglects the random component of the environment's force, and is a different model from quadratic drag or Coulomb friction outside that regime. The item asserts no value of c, no derivation of the drag law, no fluctuation theory and no measured result.

items.title: Classification of the motions of the damped oscillator by the discriminant, and nonincreasing energy $E'=-c\,x'^{2}$
items.statement:
Adopt the damped oscillator model of [[post-cm04-linear-damping-model]] with
$m>0$, $k>0$, $c\ge0$, force law $F(x,v)=-kx-cv$ and mechanical energy
$E(x,v)=\tfrac12mv^{2}+\tfrac12kx^{2}$. Write
$$\Delta:=c^{2}-4mk,\qquad \gamma:=\frac{c}{2m},\qquad \lambda_{\pm}:=\frac{-c\pm\sqrt{\Delta}}{2m}\ (\Delta\ge0),\qquad \omega:=\frac{\sqrt{4mk-c^{2}}}{2m}\ (\Delta<0),$$
and note that $\Delta=-4mk<0$ and $\omega=\sqrt{k/m}$ when $c=0$. Then:

1. **Classification and uniqueness.** Let $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an
   interval with nonempty interior. A curve $x:J\to\mathbb R$ is a motion of
   the model if and only if it is one of the following:
   - $\Delta>0$: $x(t)=Ae^{\lambda_{+}t}+Be^{\lambda_{-}t}$ for reals $A,B$;
   - $\Delta=0$: $x(t)=(A+Bt)e^{-ct/(2m)}$ for reals $A,B$;
   - $\Delta<0$: $x(t)=e^{-\gamma t}\bigl(A\cos(\omega t)+B\sin(\omega
     t)\bigr)$ for reals $A,B$.
   For every datum $(t_{0},x_{0},v_{0})$ there is exactly one maximal motion,
   it is defined on all of $\mathbb R$, and every motion with that datum is
   its restriction; when its family is written in $s=t-t_0$ instead of $t$, the coefficients
   are those supplied by clause 4 of
   [[thm-cm-homogeneous-oscillator-solution-classification]] for the shifted
   curve $s\mapsto x(t_{0}+s)$.
   In particular, for $c=0$ the motions are exactly those of the harmonic
   model of [[post-cm04-harmonic-model]] with the same $m$ and $k$.
2. **Energy dissipation.** For every motion $x:J\to\mathbb R$ the energy
   $e(t):=E(x(t),x'(t))$ is differentiable at every interior point of $J$
   with
   $$e'(t)=-c\,x'(t)^{2}\le0,$$
   and for $t_{1}<t_{2}$ in $J$ one has
   $e(t_{2})-e(t_{1})=-c\int_{t_{1}}^{t_{2}}x'(s)^{2}\,ds\le0$: the energy is
   nonincreasing on $J$. If $c>0$, then the following are equivalent: (i)
   $e$ is constant on $J$; (ii) $x'(t)=0$ at every interior point of $J$;
   (iii) $x$ is constant on $J$; (iv) $x\equiv0$ on $J$, the rest motion of
   the model. Moreover, at every interior point with $x'(t)\neq0$ one has
   $e'(t)<0$, so the energy strictly decreases there.
3. **Rest points.** The rest points of the model are exactly the pairs
   $(x,0)$ with $kx=0$, that is $(0,0)$, and the constant curve $x\equiv0$ is
   its maximal motion with datum $(t_{0},0,0)$.

The statement is read for the declared data; it asserts no value of $m,k,c$
and no empirical decay law.
items.strategy: A case deduction: transport the mathematical solution classification by the discriminant to the model, then differentiate and integrate the energy along a motion to obtain the dissipation identity, monotonicity and the characterisation of the constant-energy motions as the rest motion.
items.physical_scope: The motion classification of the damped oscillator model with m>0, k>0, c>=0: the three solution families determined by the sign of the discriminant c^2-4mk (distinct real roots, double root, oscillatory roots), uniqueness and global existence for every datum, the identity E'=-c x-dot^2 for the mechanical energy E=m x-dot^2/2+k x^2/2, nonincrease of the energy, strict negativity of its derivative when c>0 and x-dot is nonzero, and the characterisation of the constant-energy motions as the rest motion when c>0. The result is a conditional deduction from the declared model data; it asserts no value of the parameters, no measured decay and no behaviour of any real damper.

items.title: Strictly damped oscillator: explicit decay bounds, convergence to rest and asymptotic stability of the origin
items.statement:
Adopt the damped oscillator model of [[post-cm04-linear-damping-model]] with
$m>0$, $k>0$ and $c>0$ (strict damping), force law $F(x,v)=-kx-cv$ and
energy $E(x,v)=\tfrac12mv^{2}+\tfrac12kx^{2}$. Position and velocity
coordinates in every phase norm below are their normalized numerical SI
values, as defined in clause (a) of
[[def-cm04-phase-plane-and-energy-level-sets]]. For the datum
$(0,x_{0},v_{0})$, put $r_{0}:=\lVert(x_{0},v_{0})\rVert_{2}$ in that norm.
In displayed time-dependent formulas, $t$ is read numerically in seconds,
and rates in exponents are read in inverse seconds. Write
$\Delta=c^{2}-4mk$, $\gamma=c/(2m)>0$,
$\lambda_{\pm}=(-c\pm\sqrt{\Delta})/(2m)$ for $\Delta\ge0$,
$\lambda=-c/(2m)$ for $\Delta=0$ and $\omega=\sqrt{4mk-c^{2}}/(2m)$ for
$\Delta<0$. Then:

1. **Motion bounds.** For every motion $x:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ of the model
   with datum $(0,x_{0},v_{0})$ and phase norm $r_{0}$ the following bounds
   hold for all $t\ge0$, with the coefficients $A,B$ of the
   classification of [[pthm-cm04-damped-motion]]:
   - $\Delta>0$: $\lvert x(t)\rvert\le(\lvert A\rvert+\lvert
     B\rvert)e^{\lambda_{+}t}$ and
     $\lvert x'(t)\rvert\le\bigl(\lvert\lambda_{+}\rvert\lvert
     A\rvert+\lvert\lambda_{-}\rvert\lvert B\rvert\bigr)e^{\lambda_{+}t}$;
   - $\Delta=0$: $\lvert x(t)\rvert\le(\lvert A\rvert+\lvert
     B\rvert t)e^{\lambda t}$ and
     $\lvert x'(t)\rvert\le\bigl(\lvert\lambda A+B\rvert+\lvert\lambda
     B\rvert t\bigr)e^{\lambda t}$;
   - $\Delta<0$: $\lvert x(t)\rvert\le(\lvert A\rvert+\lvert
     B\rvert)e^{-\gamma t}$ and $\lvert x'(t)\rvert\le\bigl(\lvert\omega
     B-\gamma A\rvert+\lvert\gamma B+\omega A\rvert\bigr)e^{-\gamma t}$;
   and there are constants $C_{1},C_{2}>0$, depending only on $(m,k,c)$, with
   $$\lvert x(t)\rvert\le C_{1}r_{0},\qquad\lvert x'(t)\rvert\le C_{2}r_{0} \qquad(t\ge0),$$
   for the numerical SI coordinate values; equivalently the corresponding
   physical position and velocity are bounded by $(1\,\mathrm m)C_{1}r_{0}$
   and $(1\,\mathrm{m/s})C_{2}r_{0}$. Here $C_{1},C_{2}>0$ are dimensionless
   constants in the normalized SI coordinates and depend only on the
   numerical values of $(m,k,c)$ in the units declared by
   [[def-cm01-units]].
2. **Convergence.** For every maximal motion, $x(t)\to0$ and $x'(t)\to0$ as
   $t\to+\infty$ ([[def-limits-at-infinity]]).
3. **Asymptotic stability.** The rest point $(0,0)$ is Lyapunov stable and
   globally asymptotically stable in the sense of
   [[def-cm-equilibrium-and-lyapunov-stability]] for the model's phase
   system: for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $\delta>0$ such that every
   maximal motion with $\lVert(x(t_{0}),x'(t_{0}))\rVert_{2}<\delta$ for some
   $t_{0}$ is defined for all $t\ge t_{0}$ and satisfies
   $\lVert(x(t),x'(t))\rVert_{2}<\varepsilon$ for all $t\ge t_{0}$; and
   every maximal motion satisfies $\lVert(x(t),x'(t))\rVert_{2}\to0$ as
   $t\to+\infty$. The norm is the Euclidean norm on the normalized numerical
   SI coordinates of [[def-cm04-phase-plane-and-energy-level-sets]].

The constants are explicit in the proof and no value of $m,k,c$ is asserted.
items.strategy: A case deduction: bound the coefficients of the three solution families by the initial phase norm, derive the explicit decay bounds from the position estimates and the energy monotonicity, obtain convergence of position and velocity, and assemble the uniform bound that yields Lyapunov stability and the global attraction of the rest point.
items.physical_scope: The strictly damped oscillator with m>0, k>0, c>0: every motion has explicit position and velocity bounds in normalized SI coordinates, tends to zero together with its velocity, and the origin of the phase plane is a globally asymptotically stable rest point in the phase norm defined by the numerical SI coordinates. The result is a conditional deduction from the declared model data; it asserts no value of the parameters, no measured decay rate and no behaviour of any real damper, and its constants are the explicit ones produced by the classification.

items.title: The sinusoidally driven oscillator model: a prescribed external force $f_0\cos(\Omega t)$ added to the damped oscillator
items.statement:
**(i) Setting.** Work in the one-dimensional model class of
[[def-cm04-one-dimensional-models-and-equilibria]] with time window
$I_{0}=\mathbb R$, configuration domain $Q=\mathbb R$, mass $m>0$, spring
constant $k>0$ ([[post-cm04-harmonic-model]]) and drag coefficient $c\ge0$
([[post-cm04-linear-damping-model]]). Let a real **drive amplitude**
$f_{0}\in\mathbb R$ of dimension $\mu\ell\tau^{-2}$ (newtons) and an
**angular drive frequency** $\Omega>0$ of dimension $\tau^{-1}$ (radians per
second; the radian is dimensionless in the framework's angle convention,
[[def-cm01-units]]) be declared. Adopt, through the additive composition of
force contributions of clause (v) of [[post-cm02-force-superposition]] and
the external-contribution reading of [[post-cm02-interactions]], the force
law
$$F(t,x,v):=f_{0}\cos(\Omega t)-k\,x-c\,v .$$
The **sinusoidally driven oscillator model** is the one-dimensional model
with this force law; its equation of motion is
$$m\,x''+c\,x'+k\,x=f_{0}\cos(\Omega t),$$
and its data $(m,c,k,f)$ with $f(t)=f_{0}\cos(\Omega t)$ are oscillator-type
data in the sense of clause (f) of
[[def-cm04-one-dimensional-models-and-equilibria]]. The term
$f_{0}\cos(\Omega t)$ is the **drive** or **driving force**; the model is
undamped when $c=0$ and strictly damped when $c>0$.

**(ii) The drive is prescribed external data.** The driving force is a
prescribed function of time alone: it does not depend on $x$ or on $x'$, and
the object producing it is not one of the model's labels and is not modelled
dynamically. This is the same modelling status as the medium of
[[post-cm02-drag]]: the drive is an external contribution declared as part
of the model. A real apparatus, background or force generator that reacts to
the motion is **not** represented by this model; representing such a
back-reaction requires a larger model with additional states.

**(iii) Potential presentation with residual force.** The model presents its
force law through the harmonic potential $U(x)=\tfrac12kx^{2}$ with residual
force $d(t,x,v)=f_{0}\cos(\Omega t)-c\,v$, in the sense of clause (d) of
[[def-cm04-one-dimensional-models-and-equilibria]]:
$F(t,x,v)=-U'(x)+d(t,x,v)$. The mechanical energy of the model is
$E(x,v)=\tfrac12mv^{2}+\tfrac12kx^{2}$ of that clause, defined along every
motion; the model is driven and not a global potential model whenever
$f_{0}\neq0$.

**(iv) Regularity.** Let $X:=x_{\rm phys}/(1\,\mathrm m)$,
$V:=v_{\rm phys}/(1\,\mathrm{m/s})$, and $T:=t_{\rm phys}/(1\,\mathrm s)$
be the dimensionless numerical SI coordinates (the real inputs of the force
map). Write
$K:=k_{\rm phys}/(1\,\mathrm{N/m})$,
$C:=c_{\rm phys}/(1\,\mathrm{kg/s})$,
$\widehat f_{0}:=f_{0}/(1\,\mathrm N)$, and
$\widehat\Omega:=\Omega(1\,\mathrm s)$. The numerical force map is
$$\widehat F(T,X,V)=\widehat f_{0}\cos(\widehat\Omega T)-KX-CV,$$
so it is continuous and globally Lipschitz in the state variable with
numerical-coordinate constant $K+C$, uniformly in time. This is a bound on
dimensionless SI coordinates and force values, not a sum of the dimensionful
$k$ and $c$ ([[def-locally-lipschitz-in-the-state-variable]]). It is an
admissible force law of clause (a) of [[def-cm04-one-dimensional-models-and-equilibria]],
and its equation is the forced model $m\,x''+cx'+kx=f$ of
[[def-cm-oscillator-model-and-phase-system]] with the continuous function
$f(t)=f_{0}\cos(\Omega t)$.

**(v) Physical status and regime.** The model is a **restricted idealization**
adopted rather than derived: exactly sinusoidal, with constant amplitude and
frequency and no dependence on the motion. The drive amplitude and frequency
are model parameters; when their values come from an apparatus calibration,
that use is an empirical premise carrying the apparatus conditions and the
measurement uncertainty, and this item asserts no such value. The sinusoidal
form is the elementary component used by the recorded treatments; the
response to a non-sinusoidal periodic drive is a superposition statement
belonging to the mathematical theory, not an additional claim here. The
model's undamped case $c=0$ is included as a parameter value, and it is where
the resonant unboundedness of the following theorem occurs.

**(vi) Status.** Adopted assumption of the framework when a model invokes
it; it selects no law of nature on its own, and no measured response, no
resonance curve of any apparatus and no empirical resonance phenomenon is
asserted by the postulate.

items.title: The driven oscillator: steady response and amplitude profile, bounded damped and off-resonant motions, and unbounded undamped resonance
items.statement:
Adopt the sinusoidally driven oscillator model of
[[post-cm04-sinusoidal-drive-model]] with data $m>0$, $k>0$, $c\ge0$,
$f_{0}\in\mathbb R$ and $\Omega>0$, force law
$F(t,x,v)=f_{0}\cos(\Omega t)-kx-cv$ and equation
$m\,x''+cx'+kx=f_{0}\cos(\Omega t)$. Put
$$\omega_{0}:=\sqrt{\frac{k}{m}},\qquad D:=k-m\Omega^{2}+i\,c\,\Omega\in\mathbb C,$$
and define the **steady response**
$$x_{p}(t):=\operatorname{Re}\Bigl(\frac{f_{0}e^{i\Omega t}}{D}\Bigr) =\frac{f_{0}\bigl[(k-m\Omega^{2})\cos(\Omega t)+c\,\Omega\sin(\Omega t)\bigr]} {(k-m\Omega^{2})^{2}+c^{2}\Omega^{2}}\qquad(D\neq0),$$
with **amplitude** $A(\Omega):=\lvert f_{0}\rvert/\sqrt{(k-m\Omega^{2})^{2}+c^{2}\Omega^{2}}$,
and in the exceptional case $c=0$, $\Omega=\omega_{0}$ define
$x_{p}(t):=f_{0}t\sin(\omega_{0}t)/(2m\omega_{0})$. All all-time boundedness, convergence and unboundedness claims below refer to maximal motions on $\mathbb R$; local motions are their restrictions as in clause 2. Then:

1. **Steady response.** If $D\neq0$ — that is $c>0$, or $c=0$ and
   $\Omega\neq\omega_{0}$ — then $x_{p}$ is a motion of the model on
   $\mathbb R$, of period $2\pi/\Omega$, with amplitude $A(\Omega)$ in the
   sense $\lvert x_{p}(t)\rvert\le A(\Omega)$ for all $t$ and equality at
   suitable times.
2. **Reduction to the homogeneous model.** Every datum has exactly one
   maximal motion, it is defined on all of $\mathbb R$, and every motion
   $x$ of the model on an interval with nonempty interior can be written
   $x=x_{p}+y$, where $x_{p}$ is the particular motion of clause 1, or the
   resonant motion in the exceptional case, and $y$ is a motion of the damped
   homogeneous model with the same $m$, $c$, $k$ (and is a harmonic motion
   of [[post-cm04-harmonic-model]] when $c=0$).
3. **Strictly damped case $c>0$.** For every $\Omega>0$ the following hold:
  every motion is bounded on $[0,\infty)$; and
   $x(t)-x_{p}(t)\to0$ and $x'(t)-x_{p}'(t)\to0$ as $t\to+\infty$. Moreover
   $x_{p}$ is the unique motion with datum
   $(t_{0},x_{p}(t_{0}),x_{p}'(t_{0}))$ for any $t_{0}\in\mathbb R$. The
   amplitude function $\Omega\mapsto A(\Omega)$ has the following shape when $f_0\ne0$: if
   $c^{2}<2mk$ it is strictly increasing on $(0,\Omega_{*})$ and strictly
   decreasing on $(\Omega_{*},\infty)$, so has its unique maximum there, with
   $$\Omega_{*}=\sqrt{\frac{k}{m}-\frac{c^{2}}{2m^{2}}},\qquad A(\Omega_{*})=\frac{2m\lvert f_{0}\rvert}{c\sqrt{4mk-c^{2}}};$$
   if $c^{2}\ge2mk$ it is strictly decreasing on $(0,\infty)$ and does not
   attain a maximum on the declared positive-frequency domain. Its continuous
   extension to $\Omega=0$ has its maximum there. For $f_0=0$ the amplitude is
   identically zero on the domain, so every frequency has the same value.
4. **Undamped case away from resonance.** For $c=0$ and
   $\Omega\neq\omega_{0}$ every motion is bounded on $\mathbb R$.
5. **Undamped resonance.** For $c=0$, $\Omega=\omega_{0}$ and $f_{0}\neq0$
   the motion $x_{p}(t)=f_{0}t\sin(\omega_{0}t)/(2m\omega_{0})$ is unbounded
   on $[0,\infty)$, and every motion of the model is unbounded on
   $[0,\infty)$, although the drive $t\mapsto f_{0}\cos(\omega_{0}t)$ is
   bounded.
6. **Off the singular cases.** For $c>0$ the denominator never vanishes and
   every $\Omega>0$ is admissible; for $c=0$ the exceptional frequency is
   exactly $\Omega=\omega_{0}$. Consequently the boundedness assertions of
   clauses 3 and 4 hold for $c>0$, and for $c=0$ away from $\Omega=\omega_{0}$,
   and also at undamped resonance when $f_0=0$; for a nonzero drive clause 5 gives unboundedness at undamped resonance.

The statement is read for the declared model data; no value of any parameter
and no measured response is asserted.
items.strategy: A case analysis: verify the complex steady response and its real form, reduce every motion to the particular motion plus a homogeneous motion by linearity, use the strictly damped decay for the boundedness and convergence clauses, use the harmonic boundedness for the undamped off-resonant case, exhibit the unbounded resonant motion at zero damping, and read the amplitude maximum from the amplitude proposition.
items.physical_scope: The response of the driven oscillator model with m>0, k>0, c>=0, drive amplitude f_0 and angular frequency Omega>0: the explicit steady sinusoidal response and its amplitude |f_0|/sqrt((k-m Omega^2)^2+c^2 Omega^2) whenever the denominator does not vanish; the reduction of every motion to the steady response plus a homogeneous motion; boundedness of every motion in the strictly damped case, with exponential convergence of the transient to the steady response; boundedness for c=0 away from Omega=sqrt(k/m); unbounded motions at c=0 and Omega=sqrt(k/m) with nonzero amplitude, so boundedness fails exactly in the off-singular-case sense; and the positive-frequency amplitude peak when f_0 is nonzero and c^2<2mk. For c^2>=2mk and f_0!=0 the amplitude strictly decreases on Omega>0 and has no maximum on that domain; for f_0=0 it is constant. The result is a conditional deduction from the declared drive and damping models; it asserts no measured resonance curve, no value of any parameter and no behaviour of an apparatus.

items.title: Scope and limits of the one-dimensional conservative and dissipative models: declared class, approximation status, empirical parameters and open extensions
items.statement:
- **The one-dimensional class is declared, not derived.** The models of this
  page are restricted model classes of
  [[def-cm04-one-dimensional-models-and-equilibria]]: a scalar coordinate,
  a mass and a scalar force law with the standing regularity. Their relation
  to motions of the three-dimensional force branch along a straight line, or
  to effective one-dimensional reductions of constrained systems such as the
  pendulum, is a modelling identification that a consumer item states and
  uses explicitly; this page contains no three-dimensional reduction
  theorem, and the pendulum example of the companion page declares its
  effective model equation with its source support.

- **Declared assumptions versus deductions.** The harmonic, damped and driven
  models are adopted postulates
  ([[post-cm04-harmonic-model]], [[post-cm04-linear-damping-model]],
  [[post-cm04-sinusoidal-drive-model]]); every physics theorem on the page is a
  conditional deduction from those adopted models: existence and uniqueness, energy
  conservation and level-set containment
  ([[pthm-cm04-conservative-motion-and-energy]]), Lyapunov stability at a
  strict minimum ([[pthm-cm04-equilibrium-stability-at-a-strict-minimum]]),
  the sinusoid classification, energy and phase ellipses
  ([[pthm-cm04-harmonic-motion]]), the damping classification and the
  dissipation identity ([[pthm-cm04-damped-motion]]), decay and asymptotic
  stability ([[pthm-cm04-damped-decay-and-stability]]), and the response,
  boundedness and resonance statements
  ([[pthm-cm04-resonance-and-boundedness]]). No deduction here establishes
  that a real system obeys a model.

- **The harmonic model is a local quadratic approximation.** In the
  displacement coordinate $q=x-x_{*}$ centered at a strict minimum with
  $U''(x_{*})>0$, the quadratic Taylor term is
  $\tfrac12U''(x_{*})q^{2}$ after dropping the additive constant
  $U(x_{*})$. It gives the linearized equation about that minimum; the
  approximation is exact only for the declared harmonic model. For the
  pendulum, the difference
  between the nonlinear and the linearized motion is bounded only in the
  finite-time sense of
  [[prop-cm-pendulum-small-angle-linearization-bound]], with the explicit
  small-amplitude and time hypotheses of that statement; no uniform-in-time
  approximation is asserted anywhere on this page.

- **The drag is phenomenological and fluctuation-free.** The linear drag
  model is adopted for a stated viscous regime; its coefficient depends on
  body and medium; the random component of the environment's force is
  neglected. Likharev's Section 5.1, footnote 4 (Chapter 5 p. 2; PDF p. 88),
  limits that omission to oscillator energy much larger than the fluctuation
  energy scale. In the source's thermal-equilibrium setting, write
  $T\ge0$ for absolute temperature in kelvins, $k_B>0$ for the Boltzmann
  constant in joules per kelvin, $\hbar>0$ for the reduced Planck constant
  in joule seconds, and $\omega_0=\sqrt{k/m}$ in inverse seconds. The
  reported scale is $E_{\rm fluc}:=\max\{k_BT,\hbar\omega_0/2\}$, compared
  with $E_{\rm osc}:=mv^2/2+kx^2/2$ above the declared potential minimum.
  The condition is $E_{\rm osc}\gg E_{\rm fluc}$: the ratio
  $E_{\rm fluc}/E_{\rm osc}$ must be small where this approximation is used.
  The source gives no universal numerical tolerance or error estimate.
  These thermal and quantum quantities report a source's applicability
  caveat; they are not premises of the page's deterministic proofs or
  constants derived within this mechanical framework. Since the adopted
  strictly damped equation predicts $E_{\rm osc}\to0$, its exact long-time
  decay theorem does not assert indefinite physical applicability when
  $E_{\rm fluc}>0$. No fluctuation–dissipation relation, derivation of $c$
  or validity outside the linear regime is claimed; regimes of quadratic
  drag or of Coulomb friction are different models outside this page.

- **The drive is prescribed and sinusoidal.** The driving-force contribution
  is a function of time alone with an idealized sinusoidal waveform; the total
  force also includes the declared spring and drag terms. No
  back-reaction of the motion on the drive, no non-sinusoidal waveform and
  no apparatus characterization is part of the model. The boundedness and
  resonance clauses of [[pthm-cm04-resonance-and-boundedness]] are
  statements about this model's motions.

- **Measured parameters are empirical premises.** The values of $m$, $k$,
  $c$, $f_{0}$ and $\Omega$ are model data; when a value is obtained from a
  calibration or an apparatus specification, its uncertainty, the
  calibration method and the operating conditions are premises of any
  comparison with observation, and agreement of a model prediction with
  data is statistical evidence about the combined model and apparatus
  assumptions, never a proof of the model. This page asserts no measured
  value and no empirical agreement.

- **Stability conclusions and their boundaries.** The conservative model has
  a Lyapunov stable rest point at a strict minimum; the strictly damped
  model has a globally asymptotically stable rest point; the strict-minimum stability conclusion also covers degenerate strict minima, while no conclusion is drawn at other degenerate critical points, at maxima, or for the undamped driven model. In particular the linearized repulsive frequency of a maximum is
  not used to claim nonlinear instability of the model.

- **Open extensions.** Nonlinear oscillators with large amplitude (the exact
  pendulum and its secular drift), parametric resonance, nonlinear damping
  and self-oscillation, dissipative models with fluctuations, and numerical
  integration studies are outside this page's scope and belong to the later
  pages of the track; the recorded sources' treatments of those topics are
  not prerequisites of the claims proved here.

Declare the harmonic model of [[post-cm04-harmonic-model]] with the data
$$m=1\ \mathrm{kg},\qquad k=4\ \mathrm{N/m}=4\ \mathrm{kg/s^{2}},$$
time window $\mathbb R$ and configuration domain $\mathbb R$, and the datum
at $t_{0}=0$
$$x_{0}=0\ \mathrm{m},\qquad v_{0}=1\ \mathrm{m/s}.$$
The claim checked below is that the curve
$$x_{\mathrm{phys}}(t_{\mathrm{phys}})=\frac12\sin\bigl(2t_{\mathrm{phys}}/(1\,\mathrm s)\bigr)\,\mathrm m\qquad(t_{\mathrm{phys}}\in\mathbb R)$$
is the unique maximal motion of the model with this datum, that its least
positive period is $\pi$ seconds, that its energy is the constant
$\tfrac12$ joule, and that its phase curve is the ellipse
$$4x^{2}+v^{2}=1$$
in the numerical SI phase coordinates $x:=x_{\mathrm{phys}}/(1\,\mathrm m)$ and $v:=v_{\mathrm{phys}}/(1\,\mathrm{m/s})$ of [[def-cm04-phase-plane-and-energy-level-sets]]. Declare the damped oscillator model of [[post-cm04-linear-damping-model]] with
$$m=1\ \mathrm{kg},\qquad k=1\ \mathrm{N/m},$$
and the common datum at $t_{0}=0$
$$x_{0}=1\ \mathrm{m},\qquad v_{0}=0\ \mathrm{m/s},$$
for each of the three drag coefficients
$$c=1,\quad c=2,\quad c=5\qquad(\mathrm{kg/s}).$$
In displayed numerical formulas, $t:=t_{\rm phys}/(1\,\mathrm s)$,
$x:=x_{\rm phys}/(1\,\mathrm m)$, and $x'(t)$ is the numerical velocity
in metres per second; model parameters and rates are their SI numerical
values. Energy values are numerical joules, so the numerical energy identity
is $E'(t)=-c x'(t)^2$ with these conventions.
The claims checked below are that the three displayed curves are the unique
maximal motions with this datum in the three cases, that all three have
initial energy $\tfrac12$ J and satisfy $E'(t)=-c\,x'(t)^{2}$, and that the
decay bounds of [[pthm-cm04-damped-decay-and-stability]] hold with the
displayed constants:

$$\begin{aligned} c=1:\quad & x(t)=e^{-t/2}\Bigl(\cos\frac{\sqrt3\,t}{2}+\frac{1}{\sqrt3}\sin\frac{\sqrt3\,t}{2}\Bigr),\\ c=2:\quad & x(t)=(1+t)e^{-t},\\ c=5:\quad & x(t)=\frac{5+\sqrt{21}}{2\sqrt{21}}\,e^{\frac{-5+\sqrt{21}}{2}t} +\frac{\sqrt{21}-5}{2\sqrt{21}}\,e^{\frac{-5-\sqrt{21}}{2}t}. \end{aligned}$$

time $t_{\rm phys}/(1\,\mathrm s)$, and position formulas give numerical

items.title: The pendulum angle chart: stability, linearized equation, finite-time bound and quadratic-energy check
items.statement:
Adopt the **ideal planar pendulum angle-chart equation** as an effective
physical model, using the mathematical constant-metric chart of
[[def-cm-mechanical-vector-field-and-energy-in-a-chart]]. This angular chart
model is not an instance of the one-dimensional translational model class of
[[def-cm04-one-dimensional-models-and-equilibria]]:
$\theta$ is a dimensionless angle and its generalized inertia has dimension
mass times length squared. The chart data are
configuration domain $\mathbb R$, coordinate $\theta$ (the angle from the
downward vertical, in radians), effective mass parameter
$$m_{\mathrm{ef}}:=m\,l^{2}>0,\qquad\text{force law}\qquad F(\theta):=-m\,g\,l\,\sin\theta,$$
and constants $m,l,g>0$ of dimensions mass, length and length per time
squared ([[def-cm01-units]]). The force $F$ is a generalized torque. Its
equation of motion is
$$m\,l^{2}\,\theta''=-m\,g\,l\,\sin\theta,\qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad \theta''=-\frac{g}{l}\sin\theta,$$
the recorded source's point-pendulum equation (Eq. (1.18) there) expressed
with the effective inertia $m_{\mathrm{ef}}=ml^2$ and generalized torque
$F=-mgl\sin\theta$. The potential $U=-mgl\cos\theta$ is an energy-valued
scalar function of the dimensionless angle. The stability and linearization
calculations use the autonomous scalar equation as a mathematical chart
system with constant coefficient $M=m_{\mathrm{ef}}$. All phase norms mean
the Euclidean norm of the numerical pair $(\theta,(1\,\mathrm s)\theta')$;
the normalized time variable used in the finite-time estimate is
$s=t_{\rm phys}/(1\,\mathrm s)$. The claims checked below are:

1. the generalized torque is $-U'(\theta)$ for
   $U(\theta)=-mgl\cos\theta$, and $\theta=0$ is a strict local minimum;
2. the hanging rest point $(\theta,\theta')=(0,0)$ is Lyapunov stable, and
   the linearised angular equation is
   $m_{\mathrm{ef}}\theta''+mgl\theta=0$ with frequency $\omega=\sqrt{g/l}$;
3. at $g=1\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$, $l=1\,\mathrm m$, use $s=t_{\mathrm{phys}}/(1\,\mathrm s)$ and $z=(\theta,d\theta/ds)$. For every initial phase vector $z_0$ with $\|z_0\|_2=\delta=1/100$, radius $r=1/2$ and normalized horizon $T=1$, write $t$ for the numerical time $s$ in the bound. Then the difference between the exact motion and the harmonic motion with the same
   datum obeys
   $$\lVert z(t)-y(t)\rVert_{2}\le\frac{t\,e^{3t}}{12\cdot10^{4}}\qquad(0\le t\le1),\qquad\lVert z(1)-y(1)\rVert_{2}\le\frac{e^{3}}{12\cdot10^{4}} \approx1.67\cdot10^{-4},$$
   the source-supported bound of
   [[prop-cm-pendulum-small-angle-linearization-bound]];
4. the quadratic energy of the linearised angular equation,
   $E_{\rm quad}:=\tfrac12m_{\mathrm{ef}}\theta'^{2}+\tfrac12mgl\theta^{2}$,
   is not conserved along exact motions, with
   $$\frac{d}{dt}\Bigl[\tfrac12m_{\mathrm{ef}}\theta'^{2} +\tfrac12mgl\theta^{2}\Bigr]=mgl\,\theta'\,(\theta-\sin\theta),$$
   which is positive at the phase point $(\theta,\theta')=(\pi/2,1\,\mathrm{s^{-1}})$.

items.title: A bounded sinusoidal drive with unbounded motions: the undamped driven oscillator at $\Omega=\omega_0$ refutes the unqualified boundedness claim
items.statement:
In the sinusoidally driven oscillator model of
[[post-cm04-sinusoidal-drive-model]] with data $m>0$, $k>0$, $c\ge0$,
$f_{0}\in\mathbb R$, $\Omega>0$: **if the drive
$t\mapsto f_{0}\cos(\Omega t)$ is bounded, then every maximal motion of the model is
bounded on $[0,\infty)$.**
items.strategy: A direct refutation: declare the undamped driven model at m=k=f_0=Omega=1, note that its drive is bounded, exhibit the unbounded motion t sin t/2 supplied by the resonance theorem, note that every motion is unbounded, and show by contrast that the strictly damped and the undamped off-resonant cases are bounded.
items.physical_scope: A counterexample inside the driven oscillator model: with m=k=1, zero damping, nonzero drive amplitude 1 N and drive frequency equal to the natural frequency, the drive is bounded and yet every maximal motion is unbounded, so the unqualified claim that a bounded prescribed drive forces bounded motions is false. The contrast with the strictly damped parameter c=1/5 and the undamped off-resonant frequency Omega=2 shows the failure for this nonzero-drive example occurs at zero-damping resonance; at the resonant frequency with zero drive, the homogeneous harmonic motions remain bounded. The item asserts no measured value and no claim about any apparatus.
